subject: air-combat
title: Basic Fighter Maneuvers
objective: Understand one-versus-one BFM geometry, pursuit, turn performance, vertical maneuvering, energy and guns employment well enough to describe what each aircraft is doing and why.
applicability: Aircraft-agnostic concepts illustrated with US Navy T-45C training figures; type-specific numbers belong to that training example.

subject: air-combat
title: Beyond-Visual-Range Intercepts
objective: Fly the fight before the merge: read intercept geometry (target aspect, angle-off, lateral separation), put a bandit on a collision course or set up a stern conversion, understand a missile's launch zone and when to shoot, crank and decide to merge or leave, work as a section from commit to sort, and talk to the controller in bullseye and BRAA, plotting bullseye calls by hand when the cockpit has no bullseye readout, with the identification the rules of engagement require.
applicability: Fighter aircrew of every service, from the Navy's public intercept training instruction (which notes the Air Force's conventions) and the joint counterair publication, with the DCS F-16C, DCS F-14 and Falcon BMS manuals for the In the sim panel. Unclassified training principles only: real tactics, missile performance and each theater's rules of engagement and SPINS govern.

subject: sensors-situational-awareness
title: Radar, Warning Receivers and Countermeasures
objective: Understand how a fighter's pulse-Doppler radar searches, measures and locks, why PRF matters and where the Doppler notch is; point the scan volume at a called altitude; know that a radar contact has no identity until IFF or another source gives one; read a radar warning receiver and know its limits; and explain how chaff, flares and jamming defeat radar and infrared threats.
applicability: Aircrew of every service, fixed and rotary wing, from the Air Force's electronic warfare training text and the Navy's intercept training instruction, with the DCS F-16C, DCS F-14 and Falcon BMS manuals for the In the sim panel. Unclassified principles only: each aircraft's systems, threat tables and tactics manuals govern.

subject: sensors-situational-awareness
title: Situational Awareness and the Sensor Picture
objective: Build and keep situational awareness: set task priorities, run a time-shared lookout, work a mutual support contract, use infrared sensors, targeting pods and night vision goggles within their limits, use the datalink picture, use IFF to identify friends and know what a missing reply does not prove, and fuse every source into one picture you correlate and check.
applicability: Aircrew of every service, from an Air Force fighter handbook, the Navy's intercept training instruction, the Naval Academy's weapons text and joint doctrine, with Wikipedia for public datalink, IFF mode and goggle facts and the DCS F-16C and Falcon BMS manuals for the In the sim panel. Your aircraft's manuals, unit standards and the theater's procedures govern.

subject: airfield-operations
title: The Airfield and the Traffic Pattern
objective: Read a military airfield's runway numbers, markings, arresting gear, signs and lighting, read the PAPI and the Navy optical landing system, choose the runway in use from the wind, fly the overhead and the standard pattern, know where helicopters fly, make military field calls, and move safely on the ground.
applicability: Military pilots of all US services first: Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps and Army airfield practice, with shared US (FAA) standards and civil towered and non-towered procedures as supplementary. Each military field's course rules and published procedures take precedence.

subject: radio-communications
title: Radio Procedures and Phraseology
objective: Speak and understand military air–ground radio: multi-service brevity words, a training sortie's calls, call signs and preset channels, formation check-ins and training-rule calls, then the FAA technique, phonetic alphabet and numbers, contact calls, readbacks, emergency calls, transponder codes and what to do when the radio fails.
applicability: For US military pilots of all services: the joint Army, Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force brevity codes and a worked Navy training sortie first, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary US civil rule set; units and other countries differ in detail.

subject: flight-fundamentals
title: Fixed-Wing Principles of Flight
objective: Understand the four forces, lift and angle of attack, drag, control and stability, turns and load factor, stalls, the maneuvering envelope and energy well enough to explain what a military jet is doing and why.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: fixed-wing principles from Navy aerodynamics texts and its T-45 jet syllabus, with FAA handbooks as supplementary sources; worked numbers use an invented jet trainer, with US Navy T-45 training figures where cited.

subject: flight-fundamentals
title: Rotor-Wing Principles of Flight
objective: Understand how a helicopter's rotor makes lift and is controlled, from the blade's own relative wind, the collective, cyclic and pedals and the rotor systems to hover power, forward flight and dissymmetry of lift, then its hazards (retreating blade stall, vortex ring state, dynamic rollover, low G, low rotor rpm, loss of tail rotor effectiveness) and autorotation, well enough to explain what the rotor is doing and why.
applicability: For military helicopter pilots of every service: the Navy's Aerodynamics for Naval Aviators and the Army's Fundamentals of Flight first, with the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook as the supplementary source for most hazards; worked numbers use an invented utility helicopter. The type's operator's manual or NATOPS governs.

subject: navigation
title: Air Navigation
objective: Read the HSI as a picture, set up and fly a TACAN or VOR course, correct for wind, intercept courses inbound and outbound, fly DME arcs, point to point and waypoint routes, and cross-check them, with positions, headings and the navigation aids as background.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: US Navy training publications first, with the FAA AIM and Pilot's Handbook as the supplementary US civil rule set and an Army field manual for the military grid. Worked examples use the T-45C training jet's displays; your aircraft's flight manual (NATOPS or your service's equivalent) governs its systems.

subject: instrument-flight
title: Attitude Instrument Flying
objective: Fly the aircraft on instruments alone: read a panel as control and performance instruments, set attitude and power and let the lagging performance instruments catch up, fly a hub-and-spoke crosscheck without fixation or omission, recognize the illusions of spatial disorientation, and verify and recover from unusual attitudes, fixed- or rotary-wing, with or without an attitude indicator.
applicability: For military pilots of every service, fixed- and rotary-wing: the Air Force instrument flight procedures manual and the Navy's instrument training instructions, as generic technique, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary source for illusions. The figures use a generic panel and an invented flight model. Your service's instrument rules and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: instrument-flight
title: Instrument Procedures
objective: Fly an instrument sortie: the departure climb, holding and its entries, the approach to minimums, the ILS and how its needles behave, PAR and ASR radar approaches, the missed approach, high-altitude penetrations, reading the approach plate and lost communications.
applicability: For military pilots of every service, fixed- and rotary-wing: the Air Force instrument flight procedures manual and the Navy's instrument training instructions first, as generic procedure, with the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual as the supplementary US rule set. Army instrument publications could not be read for this revision; your service's instrument rules, the aircraft's flight manual and current flight information publications govern.

subject: formation-flying
title: Two-Ship Formation
objective: Fly as a section: know the parade, cruise, combat cruise and combat spread positions, hold parade by its checkpoints in altitude, bearing, closure order, make the flight's check-ins and frequency changes, fly the breakup and rendezvous and recover from an underrun, run the lost sight and blind procedures, use the lead's lights at night, and recognise the tactical turns.
applicability: For military pilots of every service: the Navy training command's T-6B and T-44C formation material as generic technique, with type numbers as examples and the FAA's lighting rule as a supplement. Air Force and Army fixed-wing formation publications are not yet covered, and helicopter formations are in their own module; your service's formation rules, unit procedures and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: formation-flying
title: Helicopter Formation
objective: Fly helicopters as a flight: know the air mission commander's, flight lead's, tactical lead's and wingmen's jobs; the staggered, echelon, trail and V fixed formations and the combat cruise, combat trail and combat spread maneuvering formations; spacing in rotor disks and vertical separation; the formation takeoff, turns, lead change and landing; and the lost visual contact, inadvertent IMC and threat breakups, lighting and the radio-silent form-up.
applicability: For helicopter pilots of every service: the US Army's fundamentals of flight training circular (TC 3-04.1-4, 2026) as generic technique, with Army-only rules labelled, and the DCS AH-64D manual for the sim. Navy and Marine Corps helicopter formation instructions were not found on a public host; your service's formation rules, unit procedures and the aircraft's operator's manual govern.

subject: air-to-air-refuelling
title: Air-to-Air Refuelling Procedures
objective: Take fuel from a tanker by boom or probe and drogue: tell the two systems apart, meet the tanker on a rendezvous from below, join Echelon Left and follow the flow around the tanker, make a boom or drogue contact and read the director lights and hose, make the refuelling calls and read the light and silent signals, and fly the breakaway and the loss of visual contact procedure, with helicopter refuelling as reference.
applicability: For tanker and receiver crews of every service and nation: NATO's standard multinational air-to-air refuelling procedures (ATP-3.3.4.2) in generic form, with sim manuals for the In the sim panel. National tanker documents, which add each tanker's limits and differences, and US service refuelling publications were not read; they, your service's rules and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Weapons Delivery
objective: Understand how an unguided weapon is delivered: the level, dive, loft and pop-up attacks and when each is used, the bombing triangle and the sight, release parameters and what an error in each does to the hit, bombing tables, low- and high-drag weapons, fuze arming and fragmentation, computed and manual sights, and the offset pop-up attack from the run-in to the recovery.
applicability: For military pilots of every service flying fixed-wing attack: the US Navy's T-45 weapons and operational navigation training instructions first, with sim manuals (DCS) for computed modes. Worked numbers are T-45 training-pattern numbers with practice bombs; your aircraft's tactical manual and your unit's rules govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Close Air Support
objective: Understand how a close air support attack is controlled and briefed: who the JTAC and FAC(A) are and who controls what, Types 1, 2 and 3 control and the bomb-on-target and bomb-on-coordinate methods of attack, the check-in, game plan and 9-line brief line by line with its readbacks, correlation, marks and talk-ons, the clearance calls, and how danger close, friendly marking and attack headings prevent fratricide, for fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft of every service.
applicability: For military aircrew of every service who fly close air support, fixed- or rotary-wing: the joint close air support publication, which all four services follow, with Marine Corps attack helicopter CAS and Army close combat attack as that publication describes them. Worked briefs are invented examples in its formats; theater special instructions, your unit's procedures and the current edition govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Precision Targeting
objective: Understand how guided weapons are put on a precise point: laser designation by the attacking aircraft, another aircraft or a ground team, laser codes, how a laser seeker finds the spot, the safety zone and attack zone around the laser target line, lasing time, what degrades a laser, coordinate-guided (GPS/INS) weapons with their accuracy and limits, target location error and its categories, and the targeting pod's part, for aircrew of every service.
applicability: For military aircrew of every service who employ laser-guided or coordinate-guided weapons, fixed- or rotary-wing, and the JTACs and FAC(A)s who work with them: the joint close air support publication's laser and inertially aided munition procedures, which all four services follow, with laser and guidance principles from the US Naval Academy's weapons systems text. The worked attack is an invented example; theater SPINS, your unit's tactics, your weapon's manual and the current edition govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: Rotary-Wing Attack
objective: Understand how attack helicopters attack ground targets: Army close combat attack and Marine Corps close air support, the rotary-wing altitude bands, low-level, contour and nap-of-the-earth terrain flight and the traveling, traveling overwatch and bounding overwatch movement techniques, holding areas, battle positions and firing points, hovering, running and diving fire with their trade-offs, which weapons suit which technique, Hellfire from a masked position, disengagement and egress, and the Army's attack by fire positions, attack methods and methods of employment, for helicopter aircrew of every service.
applicability: For military helicopter aircrew of every service who attack ground targets, and the JTACs, FAC(A)s and ground units they support: the joint close air support publication's rotary-wing tactics, which all four services follow, with Army and Marine Corps differences labelled, and an Army section from FM 3-04 and the superseded FM 3-04.126. The worked attack is an invented example; theater SPINS, your unit's tactics and your aircraft's manual govern.

subject: air-to-ground-operations
title: SEAD and DEAD
objective: Understand the suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses: what SEAD and DEAD are and how they differ, the parts of an integrated air defense system, how the radar horizon, terrain masking, engagement zones and standoff keep aircraft out of reach, the suppression methods (anti-radiation missiles, jamming, chaff, decoys and destructive attack) with their trade-offs, burnthrough and jammer geometry, and how SEAD protects a strike package, for aircrew of every service.
applicability: For military aircrew of every service who fly in, or with, a strike package against surface air defenses: the joint counterair publication, which all four services follow, with the electronic warfare principles from the US Naval Academy's weapons systems text. The worked package is an invented example; theater rules of engagement, SPINS, your unit's tactics and the current editions govern.

subject: naval-operations
title: Carrier and Amphibious Ship Operations
objective: Understand how aircraft operate from ships: the carrier's flight deck, catapults and arresting gear, who wears which jersey, the launch, Case I, II and III recoveries, the Case I pattern, the lens and the ball, LSO calls and grades, bolters, waveoffs, tanking and bingo, then amphibious assault ship operations for helicopters, tiltrotors and the AV-8B, and Army deck landing qualification.
applicability: For military pilots of every service who fly from or train on ships: Navy and Marine Corps carrier aviation from Navy training publications, Navy and Marine Corps amphibious ship procedures from the Navy's air traffic control manual, and Army helicopter shipboard operations from the Army's own field manual. Worked numbers are T-45 carrier qualification numbers; the ship's and the aircraft's NATOPS or service manuals govern.

subject: flight-planning
title: Planning a Sortie
objective: Plan a sortie from its inputs to the card you fly with: the tasking (in a joint operation the ATO, SPINS and ACO), weather, NOTAMs and charts; a nav log from true course through wind correction, variation and deviation to heading, ground speed, time and fuel; the rules of thumb for true airspeed and descent; a fuel ladder with JOKER and BINGO, reserves, alternates and the equal time point; the flight plan forms and kinds of NOTAM.
applicability: For pilots of every service: the generic method, with joint air tasking from the joint publication, planning arithmetic from an Air Force manual, and the nav log, forms and NOTAMs from FAA publications that also govern military flights in US airspace. The Navy's and Air Force's general flight rules could not be read for this revision, so service fuel reserves and alternate rules are not given; US civil rules are shown for comparison only. The worked sortie is invented; your service's rules and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: flight-planning
title: Weather and Performance
objective: Check whether the weather and the aircraft allow a plan: read a standard weather briefing in order, decode a METAR and find the ceiling, read a TAF for your arrival time, work out pressure and density altitude, say what changes takeoff and landing distance, and find the center of gravity from weights and arms.
applicability: For pilots of every service: the US METAR and TAF codes and the performance and weight and balance methods from the FAA's handbook, which US military and civil pilots share; other countries' codes differ slightly, and military weather briefing products could not be read for this revision. The jet and loads in the figures are invented; your service's weather rules and the aircraft's flight manual govern.

subject: abnormal-operations
title: Emergency Procedures
objective: Handle an in-flight emergency in any aircraft: maintain control, analyse, act and land as the emergency dictates; declare an emergency or a fuel state; fly a precautionary landing and a power-off pattern after a single-engine failure and check the glide; confirm shutdowns in a multiengine aircraft; meet fires and system failures; make the ejection decision and follow the post-ejection checklist; ditch; and handle lost radios or inadvertent cloud.
applicability: Military pilots of every service, fixed-wing, in generic form from Navy primary training squadrons' public study aids (T-6, T-44, T-45), Air Force and Navy flight rules, with the FAA's handbook and information manual as supplementary sources and Falcon BMS for the In the sim panel. Each aircraft's flight manual and checklist govern its own procedures, limits and ejection decision.
